description: The 1960 massacre that ended peaceful protest and drove the ANC underground.
content_html:
The Road to Sharpeville

By 1960, the African National Congress had spent almost half a century campaigning against racial laws through non-violent protest: petitions, strikes and civil disobedience. The Freedom Charter, adopted at Kliptown on 26 June 1955, set out a vision of a multiracial democratic South Africa. It remained the ANC's foundational document throughout the struggle.

In 1959 a breakaway group, the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), formed under Robert Sobukwe. The PAC rejected white allies and called for an Africa-first approach, targeting the pass laws as the single most hated symbol of apartheid.

Key Fact

On 21 March 1960, South African police opened fire on a crowd of approximately 5,000 unarmed protesters at Sharpeville township near Vereeniging. Sixty-nine people were killed and around 180 wounded. Most of those killed were shot in the back as they fled.

The Sharpeville Massacre

The PAC had organised a national campaign against pass laws on 21 March 1960, calling on Africans to leave their passes at home and present themselves at police stations for arrest. At Sharpeville, a crowd of around 5,000 gathered at the local police station. The exact sequence of events before the shooting is disputed; the police opened fire and continued shooting even as the crowd fled. Sixty-nine people died; the majority were shot in the back.

The images of the dead — widely circulated internationally — caused worldwide outrage. ANC president-general Albert Luthuli publicly burned his own pass card in protest. In response, the government declared a state of emergency and, on 8 April 1960, banned both the ANC and the PAC under the Unlawful Organisations Act.

Banned and driven underground, the ANC leadership debated its response to Sharpeville. A significant faction, including Nelson Mandela, concluded that half a century of peaceful protest had achieved nothing and that a new strategy was required. In December 1961, Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK, “Spear of the Nation”) was launched as the ANC’s military wing.

MK’s initial strategy was sabotage of infrastructure — power lines, government buildings and transport links — not attacks on people. Mandela and the ANC leadership made a deliberate decision to avoid killing civilians. This is important for historical accuracy: the apartheid government labelled MK as terrorists, but its founding strategy was deliberately aimed at property, not people. MK’s strategy would evolve over the following decades.

Poqo and the PAC’s Armed Response

Poqo (“Pure” or “Alone” in Xhosa) emerged as the PAC’s armed wing around 1961–62. Unlike MK’s sabotage focus, Poqo carried out attacks that included killing informers and, in some instances, white civilians. This distinction between MK’s initial strategy and Poqo’s approach is significant for understanding the range of responses within the anti-apartheid movement.

Key Fact

The immediate impact of Sharpeville: the government declared a state of emergency, banned the ANC and PAC (April 1960) and arrested thousands of activists. The long-term consequence was that both organisations were driven underground and turned to armed struggle.

Oliver Tambo slipped out of South Africa in 1960 before the banning orders took effect. He spent the next thirty years leading the ANC’s external mission from Lusaka, Zambia, building international support, running MK training camps in Angola and Tanzania, and lobbying foreign governments and the United Nations. Without Tambo’s work in exile, the ANC might have collapsed as an organisation during the “long silence” of the 1960s and 1970s.

The ANC and the Freedom Charter — Continued Relevance

Despite the banning of the ANC, the Freedom Charter continued to be circulated secretly and studied by activists. Its demand for a democratic, non-racial South Africa — with nationalisation of mines and banks, free education and equal rights regardless of race — defined the ANC’s programme. When the UDF was formed in 1983, it explicitly adopted the Freedom Charter as its guiding document, showing how the 1955 text remained alive through decades of repression.

The distinction between the ANC and the PAC remained significant throughout the 1960s and beyond. The PAC rejected working with white South Africans and focused exclusively on African leadership; the ANC maintained its multiracial approach, incorporating Coloured, Indian and white members within its alliance. Robert Sobukwe, the PAC’s founder, was imprisoned under a special “Sobukwe clause” that allowed his continued detention beyond his original sentence — a legal measure Parliament passed specifically to keep him imprisoned without trial.

The Pondoland Revolt 1960–1961

Sharpeville was the most famous episode of March 1960, but it was not the only uprising that year. The Pondoland revolt in the Transkei homeland saw rural Africans rise against hut tax increases, Bantustan control measures and forced cattle culling. The revolt was suppressed by the army and police, but it showed that apartheid was generating resistance in rural as well as urban areas. The Pondoland revolt is often overshadowed by Sharpeville in historical accounts but is significant as evidence of the breadth of opposition to apartheid.
exam_tip_html: Questions about Sharpeville often ask about its “impact” — make sure you cover both the short-term and long-term consequences. In the short term: state of emergency, banning of the ANC and PAC, mass arrests. In the long term: the turn to armed struggle, the formation of MK, the ANC going into exile. A common mistake is to focus only on international reaction and neglect the domestic consequences for the resistance movement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Sharpeville Massacre (21 March 1960) killed 69 unarmed protesters and was the turning point that ended the era of peaceful protest — the government banned the ANC and PAC within weeks.
  • Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK) was founded in December 1961 as the ANC’s military wing, initially targeting infrastructure through sabotage rather than people.
  • The anti-apartheid movement split between different approaches: ANC/MK’s sabotage strategy, Poqo’s more violent PAC methods, and Oliver Tambo’s exile diplomacy — reflecting real disagreements about how to end apartheid.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK) as founded in December 1961.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names MK as the ANC's armed wing AND gives a precise feature, e.g. its initial strategy was sabotage of infrastructure not attacks on people; or it was co-founded by Nelson Mandela. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to armed resistance. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Sharpeville Massacre of 21 March 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two precise features with detail, e.g. (1) 69 people were killed and around 180 wounded; (2) most victims were shot in the back as they fled. Secure: Two features identified, one with clear detail. Developing: Two features with limited detail. Emerging: One feature or very general response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Sharpeville Massacre was a turning point for the anti-apartheid movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons with specific evidence — e.g. banning of ANC/PAC ending legal protest; formation of MK marking the turn to armed struggle; ANC going into exile under Tambo; international outcry changing global awareness. Each reason linked clearly to 'turning point'. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two underdeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account of Sharpeville with limited explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the ANC turned to armed struggle after 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons with precise evidence — e.g. (1) decades of peaceful protest had failed to end apartheid; (2) the banning of the ANC in April 1960 made legal resistance impossible. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or descriptive answer.

practice_questions.text: Outline the events of 21 March 1960 and their immediate consequences for the anti-apartheid movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear account of the massacre (date, location, deaths) AND at least two immediate consequences (state of emergency, banning of ANC/PAC, mass arrests, Luthuli burning his pass). Secure: Correct account of events with one or two consequences. Developing: Basic account with limited consequences. Emerging: Very general or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: How far was the Sharpeville Massacre the main reason for the turn to armed struggle by the anti-apartheid movement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing Sharpeville against other factors (decades of failed peaceful protest; banning of ANC/PAC; the ideological shift within the ANC; PAC's different approach with Poqo); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of Sharpeville and the formation of MK with limited weighing of factors. Emerging: Narrative description.

knowledge_checks.q: On what date did the Sharpeville Massacre take place?
What was the initial military strategy of Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK) when it was founded in 1961?
options: Sabotage of infrastructure, not attacks on people
Armed guerrilla warfare against the police

knowledge_checks.q: The Freedom Charter, adopted at Kliptown in 1955, declared that South Africa belongs to _____ who live in it.
After Sharpeville, _____ slipped out of South Africa to lead the ANC's external mission from Lusaka, keeping the organisation alive internationally.
Match each organisation to its correct description.
right: Armed wing of the PAC, more willing to target individuals
African National Congress — multiracial liberation movement
Pan Africanist Congress — broke from ANC in 1959, Africans-only approach
Armed wing of the ANC, founded 1961, sabotage focus

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Sharpeville Massacre take place?
How many people were killed at Sharpeville?
flashcard_questions.a: 69 killed, around 180 wounded — most shot in the back

flashcard_questions.q: What campaign had the PAC organised that led to Sharpeville?
flashcard_questions.a: A national campaign against pass laws — Africans to leave passes at home and present themselves for arrest

flashcard_questions.q: When were the ANC and PAC banned?
flashcard_questions.a: 8 April 1960, under the Unlawful Organisations Act

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Freedom Charter and when was it adopted?
flashcard_questions.a: ANC founding document adopted at Kliptown in June 1955 calling for multiracial democracy

flashcard_questions.q: What does Umkhonto we Sizwe mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Spear of the Nation — the ANC's armed wing, founded December 1961

flashcard_questions.q: Who led the ANC in exile from 1960 and from where?
flashcard_questions.a: Oliver Tambo led the external mission from Lusaka, Zambia

flashcard_questions.q: What was Poqo and how did its strategy differ from MK?
flashcard_questions.a: PAC's armed wing; unlike MK it was willing to attack white civilians and informers

flashcard_questions.q: Who was ANC President-General at the time of Sharpeville and what did he do in response?
flashcard_questions.a: Albert Luthuli — he publicly burned his pass card in protest

flashcard_questions.q: Who co-founded MK and later became South Africa's first democratic president?

glossary_terms.definition: Political action that deliberately breaks unjust laws without using violence, accepting arrest as a consequence.
A document adopted at Kliptown in June 1955 declaring that 'South Africa belongs to all who live in it' and calling for equal rights regardless of race.
A movement that broke from the ANC in 1959, rejecting white involvement in the liberation struggle and insisting on an Africans-only approach.
President-General of the ANC 1952–1960 and winner of the Nobel Peace Prize in 1960 for his commitment to non-violent resistance.
ANC leader and co-founder of Umkhonto we Sizwe, who argued that the time for armed resistance had come after Sharpeville.
'Spear of the Nation' — the armed wing of the ANC, founded in 1961 to carry out sabotage against apartheid infrastructure.
The armed wing of the PAC, founded around 1961–62; more willing than MK to target white civilians and collaborators.
ANC deputy president who fled South Africa in 1960 to build the external mission in exile, keeping the organisation alive internationally until Mandela's release.
A document adopted at Kliptown in June 1955 declaring that 'South Africa belongs to all who live in it'; remained the ANC's foundational policy document throughout the struggle.
A tax levied on Black Africans in rural areas, which provoked widespread resentment and resistance during the early 1960s.
